question: What is the meaning of analysis in relation to initial design?
description: The meaning of analysis in relation to initial design involves examining the relationships among established themes to understand how different benefits and data needs interact across studies. This process helps in identifying consistent patterns and deriving higher-level design considerations that represent recurring linkages between benefits and data needs. These design considerations provide prescriptive insights into how a particular concept can be designed to support specific strategies or goals.

The findings from this process provided a detailed understanding of 
the benefits and data needs associated with DPPs, highlighting the 
practical requirements for companies seeking to capitalize on them. 
While the benefits and data needs were well-defined, the analysis also 
revealed a need for structured guidance on how to implement DPPs to 
achieve these benefits. To further structure the synthesis of findings, the 
socio-technical systems design framework presented by Maier et al. 
(1965) was applied to analyze how DPPs function within both technical 
and organizational contexts. This framework provided a lens to cate­
gorize design considerations by examining the interdependencies be­
tween four key perspectives. These perspectives provide a structured 
approach to understanding the interplay between technical, social, and 
dynamic factors in complex systems. System Scale: This perspective 
captures the scale of the system, ranging from macro-level societal im­
pacts to meso-level organizational processes and micro-level product- 
specific implementations. Effective system design requires alignment 
across these levels to ensure coherence and efficiency. Technical 
Complexity: refers to the interdependencies within the system’s tech­
nological components. This includes data handling, interoperability, 
and the scalability of platforms to accommodate evolving technical 
demands. Social Complexity: emphasizes the need for collaboration 
among stakeholders. It highlights the challenges of aligning competing 
priorities, fostering trust, and creating shared value across the value 
chain. System Unpredictability and Dynamics: This perspective addresses 
the inherent uncertainties and dynamic nature of systems. Adaptive and 
flexible design approaches are necessary to accommodate changes in 
regulations, market conditions, and technological advancements. This 
realization informed the development of the design considerations, 
which were grounded in the findings and tailored to address practical 
implementation challenges.
2.6. Analytical synthesis
After the 2nd order themes had been established, relationships 
among them were examined to understand how different benefits and 
data needs interacted across studies. This process involved comparing 
how certain themes appeared together within the same discussion or 
argument and noting when one concept was consistently described as 
enabling or influencing another. These relationships were explored 
through thematic comparison, which helped to identify consistent pat­
terns across the literature. This step resulted in an overview of the CE 
strategies, benefits of DPPs and associated data needs.
From these identified relationships, a set of higher-level design 
considerations was derived. Each design consideration represents a 
recurring linkage between benefits and data needs, articulated as a 
prescriptive insight into how DPPs can be designed to support circular 
strategies such as reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling. To situate 
these design considerations within a broader systems perspective, the 
study applied the four socio-technical perspectives—system scale, tech­
nical 
complexity, 
social 
complexity, 
and 
unpredictability. 
These 
perspectives were not part of the coding hierarchy but were used as 
interpretive lenses to clarify how the identified themes manifest in 
practice across different system contexts.
This analytical process ensured that the transition from coding to 
synthesis was systematic, and grounded in the literature. The resulting 
design considerations therefore represent the logical outcome of a 
structured process that links empirical evidence, thematic clustering, 
and interpretive abstraction.
2.7. Supplementary validation interviews
To complement the literature-based analysis, a small set of semi- 
structured interviews was conducted with industry practitioners to 
support the relevance of the design considerations identified through the 
synthesis. The participants included project managers, circularity spe­
cialists, compliance managers, and service providers involved in the 
development or adoption of DPPs. Each interview was based on a pre­
defined set of open-ended questions designed to explore key topics such 
as motivations and drivers for DPP adoption, expected benefits, types of 
data captured and required, barriers to implementation, and collabo­
ration across the value chain. The interviews were not analyzed sys­
tematically as part of the coding process but were used to assess whether 
the relationships between benefits and data needs corresponded with the 
challenges and priorities encountered in practice.
3. Findings from the literature review
The findings address RQ1, drawing on the literature review to 
identify the benefits and data needs of DPPs in enabling CE strategies.
